claims.text: The synthesis uses a near-equiatomic mixture of Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru precursors.
A relevant low-temperature synthesis can be conducted at about 180°C in ethylene glycol with a reductant and colloidal stabilizer.
Dropwise precursor addition can be compared with one-shot simultaneous addition while otherwise holding the synthesis conditions constant.
Dropwise addition slows and controls the precursor reduction kinetics.
Dropwise addition promotes more uniform atomic mixing and controlled local chemical ordering than one-pot addition.
Dropwise addition produces lower surface strain and more favorable defect distributions.
The Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru precursors have different reduction kinetics, resulting in sequential generation of their atoms during one-pot synthesis.
Different precursor reduction kinetics make one-pot synthesis prone to phase-separated nanocrystals.
Sequential addition establishes steady-state deposition and reduces the disparity among individual precursor reduction rates.
Sequential addition inhibits free-atom mobility.
Inhibition of precursor mobility during nanoparticle formation favors formation of a single HEA phase at low temperature.
Limited mobility and controlled reduction prevent phase separation and foster a uniform solid-solution alloy.
Controlled synthesis produces optimized defect and active-site distributions.
Mitigated surface strain and controlled atomic arrangement increase catalytic turnover frequency and durability.
Dropwise-synthesized nanoparticles will have a more homogeneous single-phase solid-solution structure and lower local surface strain than one-pot nanoparticles.
Dropwise-synthesized nanoparticles will exhibit greater catalytic activity and durability than one-pot nanoparticles.
One-pot nanoparticles typically have compromised catalytic performance because of phase separation or less uniform alloying.
The hypothesis applies when reduction kinetics and limited mobility dominate phase formation and active-site distribution in low-temperature solution synthesis.
Large changes in temperature, precursor concentration, solvent, or redox system may place the synthesis outside the hypothesis's applicable regime.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both structural uniformity and catalytic performance under dropwise addition would falsify the proposed explanation.
